newsitem.title: USA: New York State budget pact draws praise, criticism.
newsitem.headline: New York State budget pact draws praise, criticism.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki on Wednesday said the long-delayed budget pact he finally hammered out with lawmakers would give the state the biggest tax cuts in the nation, but critics called it a gamble.

"We are leading the nation in reducing welfare rolls, leading the nation in reducing the tax burden on our people, leading the nation in the reduction in violent crime," Pataki told reporters at a briefing. He said the tentative $68 billion pact, announced Tuesday evening, would enable New York to lead the country well into the next century.
Pataki, a Republican, said the $1.9 billion of tax cuts agreed for the current fiscal year surpassed cuts planned by each of the other 49 states.
New York State's budget is not expected to be finalized until the weekend. The pact already is 121 days late, exceeding the national record for tardiness set by New York State last year.

The agreement also drew criticism from fiscal monitors. State Comptroller H. Carl McCall, a potential Democrat challenger in next year's gubernatorial race, said only $200 million of the planned $4.75 billion in tax cuts was accounted for in the new pact. "That's a gamble -- a gamble New York has taken before and lost," he said in prepared remarks.

Bob Kurtter, a credit analyst with Moody's Investors Service, said. "Our concern is the combination of increased spending for ongoing programs coupled with tax cuts will exacerbate out-year budget gaps in years that Wall Street is not booming and the economy is not as robust."
Still, the near-term outlook for revenues was positive, he said.

Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, Democrat of Manhattan, said the state had about $2.6 billion of extra revenues this year. Silver said he was able to persuade the governor and the Republican-led Senate to agree to several of his initiatives, such as a $2.4 billion school bond act and a phase-out of the state's sales tax on clothing that cost less than $100.
He also was able to turn back Pataki's plan to cut welfare benefits over five years, though a federal five-year limit will apply.
"The fact is, we avoided harsh and inhumane cuts. We continued New York's tradition of providing for those people who have difficulty providing for themselves," he told Albany reporters.

However, the president of the New York State AFL-CIO accused Pataki of trying to divide workers into two different classes by refusing to allow welfare recipients, who have to enroll in workfare programs, to join unions.
"We have long been on record that workfare recipients should receive the rights and benefits other employees doing the same work in the same place receive," Edward Cleary said in prepared remarks.

Pataki, asked if the state could produce all of the tax cuts--including breaks on property, estate and several business taxes -- said he had succeeded in slashing taxes for three years in a row while still producing surpluses.
"So there is no question that when we make a commitment that we're going to cut taxes this year or the year after that, that is a commitment we are 100 percent confident we can and will keep."

And the governor left the door open to more tax cuts if Wall Street's boom continues, though he said the state was not counting on that. New York City's powerful financial firms contribute a large share of state and city tax revenues.
State income tax receipts only were projected to rise by five percent -- half the gain achieved in the previous year, Pataki said, noting that the state will set aside $530 million in a reserve fund.
